```{r setup, include=FALSE}
library(repair)
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse=TRUE,comment='#>')
```

`repair_leverage()` and `repair_jackknife()` are experimental options for
studying finite-sample uncertainty of a complete REPAIR analysis. Both retain
the original coefficients. They return separate results and never overwrite
the conditional covariance in the fitted analysis. Neither automatically fixes
point bias or guarantees coverage at a regularization or covariance boundary.

## Fit once, compare separate results

```{r fit}
data(repair_example)
model <- repair_lmer_refitter(score ~ day + (day | person))(repair_example$repeated)
fit <- repair(re("day") ~ practice, model, repair_example$people, "person")
ordinary <- repair_sandwich(fit)
adjusted <- repair_leverage(fit)
summary(adjusted)
```

The leverage calculation uses the same single-Gaussian-lmer scope as the full
[influence sandwich](influence-inference.html): independent target people,
contained nuisance effects, supported pointwise measurement recipes, and matching
measurement/analysis cohorts. It requires the original full influence calculation
and every deleted-system sensitivity to be usable. An unavailable correction
stays unavailable; it does not silently return ordinary influence covariance.

```{r leverage-extraction}
if (adjusted$diagnostics$full_available) {
  repair_sandwich_coefficients(adjusted)
  vcov(adjusted)
  vcov(adjusted, component="cross")
  head(adjusted$deletions)
}
```

The returned class inherits from `repair_sandwich`, so its existing extractors
apply. The inference label identifies the HC3-style correction. Person deletion
shifts, scaled sensitivity conditioning, derivative agreement and the original
HC0 identity check are retained in diagnostics. The HC3 outer products are
**uncentered**: unlike ordinary centered influence rows, their mean need not be
zero. Signed cross terms remain part of the full covariance.

## What is adjusted?

The augmented system contains measurement parameters, unweighted observed/error
moments, weighted observed/error moments, a mean-weight normalization equation,
and final corrected coefficient equations. Thus preliminary coefficients,
residual variance, structural weights and both correction multipliers all
participate in the sensitivity. Known error-free entries, including the
intercept's error variance, remain fixed at zero.

For each person, the calculation evaluates the deleted system's Jacobian at the
original fitted parameters and solves for a one-step coefficient change. For
REML the measurement block uses the exact deleted fixed-design determinant.
The covariance is the sum of uncentered outer products of these coefficient
changes. This reproduces OLS HC3 in its matching special case. No measurement
model is optimized again, and original N and policy/alpha are held fixed in the
analytic structural correction.

This is an **explicitly specified HC3-style candidate for a nonlinear augmented
system**, not a derived CR2 or Satterthwaite procedure. Nonlinear leverage
corrections depend on the representation of the equations. Mean-weight
normalization removes spurious sensitivity to a common weight in OLS; the
complete system and normalization are documented in the source repository's
`dev/leverage-jackknife-design.md`. Normal Wald intervals are the primary API.

## Delete one complete person and refit

```{r jackknife}
deleted <- repair_jackknife(fit, repair_example$repeated, repair_example$people)
summary(deleted)
```

Every deletion goes through validated `repair_refit()` replay. It removes all
observations from one target person, rekeys retained target/contained nuisance
groups, and fits the complete measurement and structural analysis on N-1 people.
Finite-N moment corrections therefore update. The scope is the single-model
deterministic draws supported by refitting, including supported nlme models;
it is broader than the initial lmer-only analytic adapter.

This requires N replacement analyses plus reference replay/validation work.
Unlike random bootstrap sampling, no person draw is generated. The caller's
standard RNG kind/state are preserved even if a callback uses RNG or fails.
Callbacks must nevertheless be deterministic fitting recipes. Hidden-state
Box-Muller and user-supplied RNGs cannot be restored and are rejected.

```{r jackknife-extraction}
head(deleted$diagnostics[,c("deleted_id","n_retained","usable","stage","measurement_singular")])
if (all(deleted$diagnostics$usable)) {
  repair_jackknife_coefficients(deleted)
  vcov(deleted)
  confint(deleted, level=.90)
}
```

The jackknife covariance is (N-1)/N times the centered cross-product of the N
delete-one coefficient vectors. Its estimated bias is reported separately and
is **not subtracted** from coefficients or interval centers. `coef(deleted)` is
the original estimate. Save either separate result with `saveRDS()`; extraction
after reloading requires no original data bindings or callback.

## Failure handling and reference distributions

Every deletion is retained in the diagnostics, including warnings, messages,
optimizer history, native singularity and moment corrections. Singular but
converged measurement fits follow the existing refit policy. If any full
coefficient vector fails, covariance and interval accessors stop explicitly.
There is no successes-only jackknife option: omitting a deletion changes the
jackknife design. Summaries and original coefficients remain inspectable.

Normal intervals are the default for both methods. An optional jackknife
`reference="t"` uses N-1 degrees of freedom as an **experimental heuristic**;
it is not a coefficient-specific Satterthwaite derivation. It can be requested
explicitly for sensitivity analysis:

```{r t-reference, eval=FALSE}
repair_jackknife_coefficients(deleted, reference="t")
```

The analytic correction can fail where a deleted sensitivity is weak or unstable.
An actual delete-one fit can switch active floors/corrections or become singular.
Those behaviors are part of the comparison, not reasons to hide inconvenient
people or select a smaller SE. More measurement rows do not substitute for more
independent people when assessing these uncertainty approximations.

The [person bootstrap](person-bootstrap.html) refits the analysis on random
N-person resamples and can describe asymmetric finite-sample distributions.
Leverage and jackknife Wald intervals still use symmetric intervals about the
original estimate. A new independent-stream six-profile simulation compares
these options; its frozen protocol, results, denominators and reproducible
evidence are archived under `dev/leverage-simulation/` in the source repository.

In that fresh 600-dataset screen, full-system HC3 improved nonzero-effect
coverage over plain IF in several difficult profiles, but its median matched
interval widths were about 1.6–1.85 times bootstrap widths and its upper width
tails were much larger. Both analytic methods returned 756/1,200 analyses;
singular original measurement fits accounted for all refusals. Delete-one
returned 1,192/1,200 but its difficult-profile Wald coverage remained about
82–92%. Person-percentile returned 1,158/1,200 with condition-dependent coverage.
These findings support inspecting bias, widths, detection and availability
together, rather than treating a finite corrected SE as a coverage guarantee.
